## Legal issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Publishing&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Legal issues")]

Main article: [Publication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publication "Publication")

Publication is the distribution of copies or [content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_(media_and_publishing) "Content (media and publishing)") to the [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_public "General public").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-bc-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-ucc-45) The [Berne Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berne_Convention_for_the_Protection_of_Literary_and_Artistic_Works "Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works") requires that this can only be done with the consent of the copyright holder, which initially is always the author.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-bc-44) In the [Universal Copyright Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Copyright_Convention "Universal Copyright Convention"), "publication" is defined in Article VI as "the reproduction in tangible form and the general distribution to the public of copies of a work from which it can be read or otherwise visually perceived."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-ucc-45)

## Privishing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Publishing&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Privishing")]

**Privishing** (_priv_ ate publ _ishing_, but not to be confused with [self-publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-publishing "Self-publishing")) is a modern term for publishing a book but printing so few copies or with such lack of marketing, advertising, or sales support that it effectively does not reach the public.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-46) The book, while nominally published, is almost impossible to obtain through normal channels such as bookshops, often cannot be ordered specially, and has a notable lack of support from its publisher, including refusal to reprint the title. A book that is privished may be referred to as "killed". Depending on the motivation, privishing may constitute a [breach of contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breach_of_contract "Breach of contract"), [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship "Censorship"),[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-47) or good business practice (e.g., not printing more books than the publisher believes will sell in a reasonable length of time).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Publishing&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/The_Caxton_Celebration_-_William_Caxton_showing_specimens_of_his_printing_to_King_Edward_IV_and_his_Queen.jpg/330px-The_Caxton_Celebration_-_William_Caxton_showing_specimens_of_his_printing_to_King_Edward_IV_and_his_Queen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Caxton_Celebration_-_William_Caxton_showing_specimens_of_his_printing_to_King_Edward_IV_and_his_Queen.jpg)

Printer working an early [Gutenberg letterpress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_letter_press "Gutenberg letter press") from the 15th century (1877 engraving)

Publishing became possible with the [invention of writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_writing "History of writing") and became more practical upon the [introduction of printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_printing "History of printing"). Before printing, distributed works were copied manually by [scribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scribe "Scribe"). Due to printing, publishing progressed hand-in-hand with the [development of books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_books "History of books").

The Chinese inventor [Bi Sheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi_Sheng "Bi Sheng") made a [movable type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type "Movable type") of earthenware c.1045, but there are no known surviving examples of his work. The Korean civil servant [Ch'oe Yun-ŭi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch'oe_Yun-%C5%ADi "Ch'oe Yun-ŭi"), who lived during the [Goryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo "Goryeo") Dynasty, invented the first metal moveable type in 1234–1250 AD.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-48)

### Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Publishing&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Europe")]

[Johannes Gutenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg "Johannes Gutenberg") developed movable type in Europe around 1450, along with innovations in casting the type based on a matrix and [hand mould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand_mould "Hand mould"). The invention of the [printing press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press "Printing press") gradually made books less expensive to produce and more widely available.

Early printed books, single sheets, and images created before 1501 in Europe are known as [incunables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incunable "Incunable") or _incunabula_. "A man born in 1453, the year of the [fall of Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople "Fall of Constantinople"), could look back from his fiftieth year on a lifetime in which about eight million books had been printed, more perhaps than all the scribes of Europe had produced since [Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_the_Great "Constantine the Great") founded his city in A.D. 330."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-49)

The [history of modern newspaper publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_newspaper_publishing "History of newspaper publishing") started in Germany in 1609, with the publication [of magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine#History "Magazine") following in 1663.

Historians describe the last third of the eighteenth century of the German book trade as the _Sturm und Drang_ period, German for "storm and stress."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-50)

Missionaries brought printing presses to [sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") in the mid-18th century.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-51)

Historically, publishing has been handled by publishers, although some authors self-published.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-52)

### United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Publishing&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: United States")]

Further information: [Books in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books_in_the_United_States "Books in the United States") and [A History of the Book in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_History_of_the_Book_in_America "A History of the Book in America")

The US publishing industry began with a printing press in Massachusetts in 1638, establishing New England as an early hub. Philadelphia also became significant, with [William Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_(printer,_born_1663) "William Bradford (printer, born 1663)") setting up the first paper mill and [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin "Benjamin Franklin") opening his own press. By the mid-19th century, New York City became the industry's center, marked by the rise of large publishing houses like [Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper_(publisher) "Harper (publisher)"), [Wiley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiley_(publisher) "Wiley (publisher)"), [Putnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G._P._Putnam's_Sons "G. P. Putnam's Sons"), and [Scribner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Scribner's_Sons "Charles Scribner's Sons"), who benefited from copyright laws and new distribution methods. Initially, they heavily relied on pirated British works until [international copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_copyright "International copyright") laws were established in 1891.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-53) The mid-19th century also saw innovations like paperback "dime novels" making literature more accessible.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-54) The post-World War I era was a boom for American publishing with new writers and publishers like [Simon & Schuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster "Simon & Schuster") and [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") emerging. The Great Depression caused a setback, but the industry recovered post-war. Since the 1960s, there's been a trend of mergers and consolidation, accelerating with the rise of online retailers and ebooks, though New York City remains a major global publishing center, home to the "Big Five" publishers (including [HarperCollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HarperCollins "HarperCollins"), [Penguin Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Random_House "Penguin Random House"), and [Simon & Schuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster "Simon & Schuster")) and major educational publishers like [Macmillan Learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macmillan_Learning "Macmillan Learning"), [McGraw-Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGraw-Hill_Education "McGraw-Hill Education"), [Scholastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholastic_Corporation "Scholastic Corporation"), and [Wiley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiley_(publisher) "Wiley (publisher)"), alongside numerous independent publishers.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-55) Starting with [Cornell University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University_Press "Cornell University Press") in 1869 and [Johns Hopkins University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University_Press "Johns Hopkins University Press") in 1878, many universities set up publishing houses to publish scholarly books and journals of this sort produced by their faculty and graduate students. In the 21st century, however, financial pressures. have been reducing their output.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-56)

A U.S.-based study in 2016 that surveyed 34 publishers found that straight, able-bodied, white females overwhelmingly represent the publishing industry in the US.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-57)[_Salon_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_(website) "Salon (website)") described the situation as a "lack of diversity behind the scenes in book world."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-58) A survey in 2020 by the same group found there has been no significant statistical change in the lack of diversity since the 2016 survey.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-59) Lack of diversity in the American publishing industry has been an issue for years. Within the industry, the least amount of diversity was in higher-level editorial positions.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers#cite_note-60)

### Internet Age

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Publishing&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Internet Age")]

The [establishment of the World Wide Web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_World_Wide_Web "History of the World Wide Web") in 1989 soon propelled the [website](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Website "Website") into a dominant publishing medium. [Wikis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_wikis "History of wikis") and [blogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_blogging "History of blogging") soon developed, followed by [online books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_book "Online book"), [online newspapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_newspaper#History "Online newspaper"), and [online magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_magazine "Online magazine"). This also facilitated the [technological convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technological_convergence "Technological convergence") of commercial and self-published content and the convergence of publishing and production into [online production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_producer "Online producer") through the development of [multimedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multimedia "Multimedia") content.

[Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_High_School_for_Science_and_Technology "Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology") in [Fairfax, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax,_Virginia "Fairfax, Virginia"), one of the highest rated magnet schools in the United States

In [the U.S. education system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_the_United_States "Education in the United States"), **magnet schools** are [public schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_school "State school") with [specialized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specialized_school "Specialized school")[courses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Course_(education) "Course (education)") or [curricula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curriculum "Curriculum"). Normally, a student will attend an elementary school, and this also determines the middle school and high school they attend unless they move. "[Magnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet "Magnet")" refers to how magnet schools accept students from different areas, pulling students out of the normal progression of schools. Attending them is voluntary.

There are magnet schools at the [elementary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_school "Elementary school"), [middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_school "Middle school"), and [high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_school "High school") levels. In the United States, where education is [decentralized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decentralization "Decentralization"), some magnet schools are established by [school districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_district "School district") and draw only from the district, while others are set up by [state governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_governments_of_the_United_States "State governments of the United States") and may draw from multiple [districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District "District"). Other magnet programs are within [comprehensive schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_school "Comprehensive school"), as is the case with several "schools within a school". In large urban areas, several magnet schools with different specializations may be combined into a single "center," such as [Skyline High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyline_High_School_(Dallas) "Skyline High School (Dallas)") in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas").

Other countries have similar types of schools, such as [specialist schools in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specialist_schools_in_the_United_Kingdom "Specialist schools in the United Kingdom"). Most of these are academically selective. Other schools are built around elite sporting programs or teach agricultural skills such as farming or animal husbandry.

In 1965, then [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Vice_President "United States Vice President")[Hubert Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey "Hubert Humphrey") came to [John Bartram High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bartram_High_School "John Bartram High School") in [Southwest Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Philadelphia "Southwest Philadelphia") to declare it the first magnet school in the country. Bartram's curriculum was concentrated in the commercial field, offering commercial and business training to students from all over Philadelphia.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnet_school&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In the United States, the term "magnet school" refers to public schools with enrichment programs that are designed to attract and serve certain targeted subgroups of potential students and their families. There are two major categories of public magnet school structures in the United States, and although there is some overlap, their origins and missions remain largely distinct. The first type of magnet school is the fully competitive admissions magnet school. These schools use competitive admissions, usually rely on a standardized assessment score, and are structured to serve and support populations that are 100% gifted and/or talented students. Schools in this group generally rank among the top 100 public high schools in the United States. Examples of this type of school and program include the [Maine School of Science and Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_School_of_Science_and_Mathematics "Maine School of Science and Mathematics"), [Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_High_School_for_Science_and_Technology "Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology") in Virginia, [The School Without Walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_School_Without_Walls_(Washington,_D.C.) "The School Without Walls (Washington, D.C.)") in the District of Columbia, and nine schools that all use competitive admissions and are overseen by the New York City Department of Education (which still uses the older term "[specialized school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specialized_high_schools_in_New_York_City "Specialized high schools in New York City")" instead of "magnet school" to refer to them[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]). In addition, [Chicago Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Public_Schools "Chicago Public Schools") uses the term "selective enrollment[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-1)" instead of "magnet school". Another type of "magnet school" or "magnet program" emerged in the United States in the 1970s[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-2) as one means of remedying [racial segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation "Racial segregation") in public schools, and they were written into law in Section 5301 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Authorization.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-3) Demographic trends following the 1954 _[Brown v. Board of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown\_v.\_Board\_of\_Education "Brown v. Board of Education")_[US Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Supreme_Court "US Supreme Court") decision revealed a pattern later characterized as [white flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight"), the [hypersegregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersegregation "Hypersegregation") of blacks and whites, as the latter moved to the [suburbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburb "Suburb").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-5) The first magnet school, McCarver Elementary School, opened in [Tacoma, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma,_Washington "Tacoma, Washington"), in 1968.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-6) This second type of magnet can often take the form of "a school within a school," meaning that the school may have no competitive admissions for the majority of the school population, and even the magnet program itself may not have fully competitive admissions. This is consistent with the equity-based objectives of such programs.

With the magnets designed to increase equity, at first school districts tried using involuntary plans which involved court-ordered attendance, the [bussing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desegregation_busing "Desegregation busing") of children far from their homes, and building closer schools to achieve the required balance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-7) Later, voluntary school integration plans were developed. One approach that educators within the public school system came up with was open schools. During the Open Schools movement of the 1970s, several ideas designed to influence public education were put into practice, including Schools without Walls, Schools within a School, Multicultural Schools, Continuation Schools, Learning Centers, Fundamental Schools, and Magnet Schools.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-lange2002-8) "These schools were characterized by parent, student, and teacher choice, autonomy in learning and pace, non-competitive evaluation, and a child centered approach."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-lange2002-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-9) Magnet schools have been the most successful of the ideas that originated from the Open Schools movement. It was expounded in 1971 by educator Nolan Estes, superintendent of [Dallas Independent School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Independent_School_District "Dallas Independent School District").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-10) The [Magnet Schools Assistance Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_Schools_Assistance_Program "Magnet Schools Assistance Program") was developed in the early 1980s as a way to encourage schools to address _[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_facto "De facto")_ racial segregation. Funds were given to school districts that implemented voluntary desegregation plans or court orders to reduce racial isolation.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-11)

From 1985 to 1999, a [US district court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_district_court "US district court") judge required the state of [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") to fund the creation of magnet schools in the [Kansas City Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Public_Schools "Kansas City Public Schools") to reverse the [white flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight") that had afflicted the school district since the 1960s. The district's annual budget more than tripled in the process. The expenditure per pupil and the student–teacher ratio were the best of any major school district in the nation. Many high schools were given college-level facilities. Still, test scores in the magnet schools did not rise; the black–white gap did not diminish; and there was less, not greater, integration.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-12) Finally, on September 20, 2011, The Missouri Board of Education voted unanimously to withdraw the district's [educational accreditation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_accreditation "Educational accreditation") status from January 1, 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-13)

Districts started embracing the magnet school models in the hope that their geographically open admissions would end racial segregation in "good" schools and decrease _de facto_ segregation of schools in poorer areas. To encourage the voluntary desegregation, districts started developing magnet schools to draw students to specialized schools all across their districts. Each magnet school would have a specialized curriculum that would draw students based on their interests. One of the goals of magnet schools is to eliminate, reduce, and prevent minority group isolation while providing the students with a stronger knowledge of academic subjects and vocational skills.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-14)

Within a few years, in locations such as [Richmond, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia"), additional magnet school programs for children with special talents were developed at facilities in locations that parents would have otherwise found undesirable. That effort to both attract voluntary enrollment and achieve the desired racial balance met with considerable success and helped improve the acceptance of farther distances, hardships with transportation for extracurricular activities, and the separation of siblings. Even as districts such as Richmond were released from desegregation court orders, the parental selection of magnet school programs has continued to create more racially diverse schools than would have otherwise been possible. With a wide range of magnet schools available, a suitable program could be found for more children than only the "bright" ones for whom the earliest efforts were directed.

Some 21st-century magnet schools have de-emphasized the racial integration aspects, such as Capital Prep Magnet School, a high school in [Hartford, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut "Hartford, Connecticut").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-hartford-15) Capital Prep, a year-round school where more than 80% of its students are black and Latino, boasts a near-0% dropout rate; 100% of its 2009 senior class was sent to a four-year college.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-hartford-15) According to the school's principal, the goal is to prepare all of its students for college.

Since coming into fruition, the number of magnet schools has risen dramatically. Over 232 school districts housed magnet school programs in the early 1990s. By the end of the decade, nearly 1,400 magnet schools were operating across the country.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-16)

Traditionally, these magnet schools are found in neighborhoods with large minority populations. They advertise their unique educational curricula in order to attract white students who do not live in the surrounding area. In this way, the schools act as a "magnet" pulling out-of-neighborhood students that would otherwise go to a school in their traditional attendance zone.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-17)

Some magnet schools have a competitive entrance process, requiring an [entrance examination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrance_examination "Entrance examination"), [interview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interview "Interview"), or [audition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audition_(performing_arts) "Audition (performing arts)"). Other magnet schools either select all students who apply, or use a [lottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lottery "Lottery") system among students who apply, while others combine elements of competitive entrance and a lottery among applicants.

Most magnet schools concentrate on a particular discipline or area of study, while others (such as [International Baccalaureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Baccalaureate "International Baccalaureate") schools) have a more general focus. Magnet programs may focus on academics ([mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics"), [natural sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_science "Natural science"), and [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering"); [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities"); [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_sciences "Social sciences"); [fine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_art "Fine art") or [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts")) or may focus on [technical/vocational/agricultural education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocational_education "Vocational education").

Access to free transportation is a key component in facilitating racial diversity in magnet schools. According to a survey distributed at the Magnet Schools of America's (MSA) 2008 annual meeting, in magnet schools with free transportation services, non-white students comprise almost 33% of the student body, which is higher than the 23% found in magnet schools without such services. Moreover, 11.9% of magnet schools that do not provide transportation are largely one-race, while only 6.4% of magnet schools with the provision of transportation are characterized as one-race schools. Such services are integral in ensuring that potential out-of-neighborhood students have access to these schools of choice. Ultimately, the presence of free transportation contributes to more integrated magnet environments.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-18)

Across the country, magnet school application forms assume that its readers are proficient in reading and writing in English, understand the school's curriculum, and recognize what kinds of resources are offered to students at that respective school. In diverse urban contexts especially, these assumptions privilege some families over others. Parents who seek out magnet schools tend to be Asian, educated, middle-class, and English-fluent. Thus, in order to break down the racial disparities these schools were intended to dismantle, magnet school programs have to be intentional in not only their outreach efforts, but also how they create the application text itself.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-19)

Public schools with specialized courses or curricula

[Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_High_School_for_Science_and_Technology "Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology") in [Fairfax, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax,_Virginia "Fairfax, Virginia"), one of the highest rated magnet schools in the United States

In [the U.S. education system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_the_United_States "Education in the United States"), **magnet schools** are [public schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_school "State school") with [specialized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specialized_school "Specialized school")[courses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Course_(education) "Course (education)") or [curricula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curriculum "Curriculum"). Normally, a student will attend an elementary school, and this also determines the middle school and high school they attend unless they move. "[Magnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet "Magnet")" refers to how magnet schools accept students from different areas, pulling students out of the normal progression of schools. Attending them is voluntary.

There are magnet schools at the [elementary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_school "Elementary school"), [middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_school "Middle school"), and [high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_school "High school") levels. In the United States, where education is [decentralized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decentralization "Decentralization"), some magnet schools are established by [school districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_district "School district") and draw only from the district, while others are set up by [state governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_governments_of_the_United_States "State governments of the United States") and may draw from multiple [districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District "District"). Other magnet programs are within [comprehensive schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_school "Comprehensive school"), as is the case with several "schools within a school". In large urban areas, several magnet schools with different specializations may be combined into a single "center," such as [Skyline High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyline_High_School_(Dallas) "Skyline High School (Dallas)") in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas").

Other countries have similar types of schools, such as [specialist schools in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specialist_schools_in_the_United_Kingdom "Specialist schools in the United Kingdom"). Most of these are academically selective. Other schools are built around elite sporting programs or teach agricultural skills such as farming or animal husbandry.

In 1965, then [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Vice_President "United States Vice President")[Hubert Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey "Hubert Humphrey") came to [John Bartram High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bartram_High_School "John Bartram High School") in [Southwest Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Philadelphia "Southwest Philadelphia") to declare it the first magnet school in the country. Bartram's curriculum was concentrated in the commercial field, offering commercial and business training to students from all over Philadelphia.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnet_school&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/DeBakeyHSnewbldg.jpg/250px-DeBakeyHSnewbldg.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DeBakeyHSnewbldg.jpg)

[DeBakey High School for Health Professions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeBakey_High_School_for_Health_Professions "DeBakey High School for Health Professions") in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), is a magnet school specializing in medical sciences

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Magnet2.jpg/250px-Magnet2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Magnet2.jpg)

These 2nd graders from Buchanan Math Science Magnet School in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), work on an art project. After studying the physical environment of the planet Mars, they are now designing a suitable Martian community.

In the United States, the term "magnet school" refers to public schools with enrichment programs that are designed to attract and serve certain targeted subgroups of potential students and their families. There are two major categories of public magnet school structures in the United States, and although there is some overlap, their origins and missions remain largely distinct. The first type of magnet school is the fully competitive admissions magnet school. These schools use competitive admissions, usually rely on a standardized assessment score, and are structured to serve and support populations that are 100% gifted and/or talented students. Schools in this group generally rank among the top 100 public high schools in the United States. Examples of this type of school and program include the [Maine School of Science and Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_School_of_Science_and_Mathematics "Maine School of Science and Mathematics"), [Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_High_School_for_Science_and_Technology "Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology") in Virginia, [The School Without Walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_School_Without_Walls_(Washington,_D.C.) "The School Without Walls (Washington, D.C.)") in the District of Columbia, and nine schools that all use competitive admissions and are overseen by the New York City Department of Education (which still uses the older term "[specialized school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specialized_high_schools_in_New_York_City "Specialized high schools in New York City")" instead of "magnet school" to refer to them[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]). In addition, [Chicago Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Public_Schools "Chicago Public Schools") uses the term "selective enrollment[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-1)" instead of "magnet school". Another type of "magnet school" or "magnet program" emerged in the United States in the 1970s[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-2) as one means of remedying [racial segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation "Racial segregation") in public schools, and they were written into law in Section 5301 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Authorization.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-3) Demographic trends following the 1954 _[Brown v. Board of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown\_v.\_Board\_of\_Education "Brown v. Board of Education")_[US Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Supreme_Court "US Supreme Court") decision revealed a pattern later characterized as [white flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight"), the [hypersegregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersegregation "Hypersegregation") of blacks and whites, as the latter moved to the [suburbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburb "Suburb").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-5) The first magnet school, McCarver Elementary School, opened in [Tacoma, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma,_Washington "Tacoma, Washington"), in 1968.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-6) This second type of magnet can often take the form of "a school within a school," meaning that the school may have no competitive admissions for the majority of the school population, and even the magnet program itself may not have fully competitive admissions. This is consistent with the equity-based objectives of such programs.

With the magnets designed to increase equity, at first school districts tried using involuntary plans which involved court-ordered attendance, the [bussing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desegregation_busing "Desegregation busing") of children far from their homes, and building closer schools to achieve the required balance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-7) Later, voluntary school integration plans were developed. One approach that educators within the public school system came up with was open schools. During the Open Schools movement of the 1970s, several ideas designed to influence public education were put into practice, including Schools without Walls, Schools within a School, Multicultural Schools, Continuation Schools, Learning Centers, Fundamental Schools, and Magnet Schools.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-lange2002-8) "These schools were characterized by parent, student, and teacher choice, autonomy in learning and pace, non-competitive evaluation, and a child centered approach."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-lange2002-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-9) Magnet schools have been the most successful of the ideas that originated from the Open Schools movement. It was expounded in 1971 by educator Nolan Estes, superintendent of [Dallas Independent School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Independent_School_District "Dallas Independent School District").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-10) The [Magnet Schools Assistance Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_Schools_Assistance_Program "Magnet Schools Assistance Program") was developed in the early 1980s as a way to encourage schools to address _[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_facto "De facto")_ racial segregation. Funds were given to school districts that implemented voluntary desegregation plans or court orders to reduce racial isolation.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-11)

From 1985 to 1999, a [US district court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_district_court "US district court") judge required the state of [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") to fund the creation of magnet schools in the [Kansas City Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Public_Schools "Kansas City Public Schools") to reverse the [white flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight") that had afflicted the school district since the 1960s. The district's annual budget more than tripled in the process. The expenditure per pupil and the student–teacher ratio were the best of any major school district in the nation. Many high schools were given college-level facilities. Still, test scores in the magnet schools did not rise; the black–white gap did not diminish; and there was less, not greater, integration.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-12) Finally, on September 20, 2011, The Missouri Board of Education voted unanimously to withdraw the district's [educational accreditation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_accreditation "Educational accreditation") status from January 1, 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-13)

Districts started embracing the magnet school models in the hope that their geographically open admissions would end racial segregation in "good" schools and decrease _de facto_ segregation of schools in poorer areas. To encourage the voluntary desegregation, districts started developing magnet schools to draw students to specialized schools all across their districts. Each magnet school would have a specialized curriculum that would draw students based on their interests. One of the goals of magnet schools is to eliminate, reduce, and prevent minority group isolation while providing the students with a stronger knowledge of academic subjects and vocational skills.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-14)

Within a few years, in locations such as [Richmond, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia"), additional magnet school programs for children with special talents were developed at facilities in locations that parents would have otherwise found undesirable. That effort to both attract voluntary enrollment and achieve the desired racial balance met with considerable success and helped improve the acceptance of farther distances, hardships with transportation for extracurricular activities, and the separation of siblings. Even as districts such as Richmond were released from desegregation court orders, the parental selection of magnet school programs has continued to create more racially diverse schools than would have otherwise been possible. With a wide range of magnet schools available, a suitable program could be found for more children than only the "bright" ones for whom the earliest efforts were directed.

Some 21st-century magnet schools have de-emphasized the racial integration aspects, such as Capital Prep Magnet School, a high school in [Hartford, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut "Hartford, Connecticut").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-hartford-15) Capital Prep, a year-round school where more than 80% of its students are black and Latino, boasts a near-0% dropout rate; 100% of its 2009 senior class was sent to a four-year college.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-hartford-15) According to the school's principal, the goal is to prepare all of its students for college.

Since coming into fruition, the number of magnet schools has risen dramatically. Over 232 school districts housed magnet school programs in the early 1990s. By the end of the decade, nearly 1,400 magnet schools were operating across the country.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-16)

Traditionally, these magnet schools are found in neighborhoods with large minority populations. They advertise their unique educational curricula in order to attract white students who do not live in the surrounding area. In this way, the schools act as a "magnet" pulling out-of-neighborhood students that would otherwise go to a school in their traditional attendance zone.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-17)

## Enrollment and curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnet_school&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Enrollment and curriculum")]

Some magnet schools have a competitive entrance process, requiring an [entrance examination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrance_examination "Entrance examination"), [interview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interview "Interview"), or [audition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audition_(performing_arts) "Audition (performing arts)"). Other magnet schools either select all students who apply, or use a [lottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lottery "Lottery") system among students who apply, while others combine elements of competitive entrance and a lottery among applicants.

Most magnet schools concentrate on a particular discipline or area of study, while others (such as [International Baccalaureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Baccalaureate "International Baccalaureate") schools) have a more general focus. Magnet programs may focus on academics ([mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics"), [natural sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_science "Natural science"), and [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering"); [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities"); [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_sciences "Social sciences"); [fine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_art "Fine art") or [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts")) or may focus on [technical/vocational/agricultural education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocational_education "Vocational education").

Access to free transportation is a key component in facilitating racial diversity in magnet schools. According to a survey distributed at the Magnet Schools of America's (MSA) 2008 annual meeting, in magnet schools with free transportation services, non-white students comprise almost 33% of the student body, which is higher than the 23% found in magnet schools without such services. Moreover, 11.9% of magnet schools that do not provide transportation are largely one-race, while only 6.4% of magnet schools with the provision of transportation are characterized as one-race schools. Such services are integral in ensuring that potential out-of-neighborhood students have access to these schools of choice. Ultimately, the presence of free transportation contributes to more integrated magnet environments.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-18)

Across the country, magnet school application forms assume that its readers are proficient in reading and writing in English, understand the school's curriculum, and recognize what kinds of resources are offered to students at that respective school. In diverse urban contexts especially, these assumptions privilege some families over others. Parents who seek out magnet schools tend to be Asian, educated, middle-class, and English-fluent. Thus, in order to break down the racial disparities these schools were intended to dismantle, magnet school programs have to be intentional in not only their outreach efforts, but also how they create the application text itself.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet_school#cite_note-19)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American educator (1866–1938)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Portrait_of_Henry_Alexander_Hunt.png/250px-Portrait_of_Henry_Alexander_Hunt.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_Henry_Alexander_Hunt.png)

A photo of Henry Alexander Hunt featured in the August 1930 edition of _[The Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crisis "The Crisis")_ magazine. The photo accompanied an article discussing Hunt being awarded the 16th [Spingarn Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal "Spingarn Medal").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-1)

**Henry Alexander Hunt** (October 10, 1866[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-2)– October 1, 1938) was an American educator who led efforts to reach blacks in rural areas of Georgia. He was awarded the [Spingarn Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal "Spingarn Medal") by the [National Association for the Advancement of Colored People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People "National Association for the Advancement of Colored People") (NAACP), as well as the Harmon Prize. In addition, he was recruited in the 1930s by President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") to join the president's [Black Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Cabinet "Black Cabinet"), an informal group of more than 40 prominent African Americans appointed to positions in the executive agencies.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Henry A. Hunt was born on October 10, 1866, to parents Henry Alexander Hunt Sr. and Mariah Hunt.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-3) He was born on "Hunt Hill", by the small town of Sparta, in [Hancock County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hancock_County,_Georgia "Hancock County, Georgia"), part of the [Black Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Belt_(geological_formation) "Black Belt (geological formation)"). Hunt was the youngest of eight children, four boys and four girls, born to an African-American mother, Mariah Hunt. The Hunts lived in a weather-beaten house on their small farm and the children grew up working on the farm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) Despite his African-American roots, Hunt's appearance led people to assume he was from purely Caucasian descent. After Hunt's death, [W. E. B. Du Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois "W. E. B. Du Bois"), a personal friend of his, publicly spoke of Hunt's Caucasian appearance and reflected on the questions Hunt received about why he did not choose to hide his mixed-race background.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Du_Bois-1940-5)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]

He attended school at Sparta for his early education. In 1882, at the age of 16, he started at [Atlanta University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_University "Atlanta University") (now Clark Atlanta University), one of the [historically black colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges "Historically black colleges") created after the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6) While attending [Atlanta University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Atlanta_University "Clark Atlanta University"), Hunt met Florence Johnson, the woman he would eventually marry in 1893.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-van_Hartesveldt-2015-7)[Edward A. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_A._Johnson "Edward A. Johnson"), Florence's brother, was the former Assemblyman of New York.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Horne%E2%80%931930-8)

Throughout his time as a college student, including vacations from school, Hunt worked as a carpenter to earn money.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) Hunt graduated from [Atlanta University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Atlanta_University "Clark Atlanta University") with a Bachelors of Arts degree and completion of coursework in the Industrial Department in 1890.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early career")]

Hunt worked for the education of black students for his entire career. After graduating, he had a job offer in Africa, but he turned this down to be the principal at Charlotte Grade School in Charlotte, North Carolina.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) He stayed at this position for less than a year, leaving the Charlotte Grade School in 1891 for the position of Superintendent of the Industrial Department at [Biddle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biddle_University "Biddle University") (now [Johnson C. Smith University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_C._Smith_University "Johnson C. Smith University")). In the year 1900, Hunt established an annual African-American farmer's conference including the counties surrounding Charlotte, North Carolina.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6) Hunt continued to work for [Biddle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biddle_University "Biddle University") for the rest of the thirteen and a half years the Hunts were in Charlotte, North Carolina.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) By the time he left Biddle University, he had also been appointed as Superintendent of Boarding.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9)

### Fort Valley career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Fort Valley career")]

He was then the principal of [Fort Valley High and Industrial School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley_High_and_Industrial_School "Fort Valley High and Industrial School"), [Fort Valley, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley,_Georgia "Fort Valley, Georgia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Horne%E2%80%931930-8)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-10) The [Fort Valley High and Industrial School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley_High_and_Industrial_School "Fort Valley High and Industrial School"), affiliated with the American Church Institute of the [Protestant Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)"), was chartered in 1895, but struggled financially.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-11) The school received funds from Northern philanthropists, but there were disagreements about whether the school should pursue a Liberal Arts educational model or the Hampton-Tuskegee Industrial educational model.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) In the 1902–1903 school year, the school's first principal, John W. Davis was released as principal and the trustees began looking for replacements.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) George Foster Peabody, one of Fort Valley's Northern philantrhopists who was on the Board of Trustees, suggested Hunt because of his work at Biddle University. Other trustees had suggested different men for the position of principal, and although Hunt was among the final three candidates, he was only offered the position after the other two had declined the job.

Even after this, Hunt did not immediately get the job. The trustees were reluctant to hire an Atlanta University graduate since [Booker T. Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._Washington "Booker T. Washington") had advised the board of trustees that an Industrial College not run by a [Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_University "Hampton University") or [Tuskegee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_University "Tuskegee University") graduate, was not likely to be successful.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) The 1903 school year began for Fort Valley High and Industrial School began without a principal as the trustees continued to scrutinize Hunt. Hunt stressed the mechanical background he acquired from his industrial studies at Atlanta University and his background in carpentry and was then hired in November 1903.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) The Hunts moved to Fort Valley with their three small children, two girls and one boy, and Hunt began his career as the Fort Valley High and Industrial School principal on February 9, 1904.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9)

When the Hunts came to the school it consisted of a single building, Odd Fellows Lodge, and the school had an annual budget of $840.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-van_Hartesveldt-2015-7) The Hunts lived with no running water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-van_Hartesveldt-2015-7) Hunt began to change the school's educational model to aim more towards vocational training and trade-based studies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) Hunt instated classes in sewing, cooking, carpentry, and gardening. Hunt also planted two hundred peach trees (Fort Valley is located in what is known as the [Peach Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Belt_Conference "Peach Belt Conference")) to expand the agricultural program to include practical and demonstrative agricultural education.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) Hunt felt a focus on agricultural studies was important given the emphasis on and prevalence of agriculture in middle Georgia, where the school was located. In the beginning and throughout Hunt's career the area surrounding the school was dominated by a population of African Americans who worked in agriculture. Hunt often stated his goal as empowering the African Americans attending Fort Valley, as well as the surrounding African-American community, to become effective in their trade.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9)

> With Negroes cultivating millions of acres of land, surely no argument is needed to prove the wisdom and the justice of giving them every possible opportunity to learn how to do that work more intelligently and with greater skill.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

In 1907, Hunt presented to the Board of Trustees the need to add the study of scientific agricultural training to the existing agricultural studies program.

> Working as we do among a people who are engaged very largely in agriculture it would seem to be not only important but absolutely necessary that special inducements be held out to students who wish to give attention to this particular line of work.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

Also in 1907, Hunt began an annual Fort Valley conference for African American farmers. The conference brought experts from throughout the state, the country and some of the top industrial schools such as [Tuskegee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_University "Tuskegee University"), to inform the attendees of the latest agricultural technology and information. At these conferences, Hunt stressed the possibility for African-American farmers to own their farms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) In 1907, Hunt also began a practical agricultural program, with the help of the [United States Department of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture "United States Department of Agriculture"), five acres of land were cultivated and used as part of the educational process through demonstrations.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) With financial help from the General Board of Education, Hunt added 55 acres to the school's educational farmland in 1915.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) Hunt's reputation as an advocate for the African-American farmer spread. In 1918, the Governor of Georgia, [Hugh M. Dorsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Dorsey "Hugh Dorsey"), appointed Hunt to the position of supervisor of Negro economics for the state of Georgia. In this position Hunt focused on problems relating to agricultural labor in Georgia.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

In 1925, [W. E. B. Du Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois "W. E. B. Du Bois") asked for Hunt's help with a research project focused on the study of Negro Common Schools in Georgia. In a response letter to Du Bois, Hunt expressed interest but ultimately declined the offer because he was busy overseeing the building of a boy's dormitory on the Fort Valley campus.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-12)

In 1930, Hunt was awarded the 16th Spingarn Medal for his 25 years of work in Fort Valley. When he started working for Fort Valley High and Industrial School there was only one building. Over the years, he raised funds to build the plant of the school and turned it into a community center of teaching about health and farming, as well as academic subjects, and built relations with the regional community of 300,000 blacks and whites. The result of this was a campus expanded to 12 buildings, 91 acres of land, and a worth of $450,000 in 1930.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Horne%E2%80%931930-8) In 1931 Hunt received the [Julius Rosenwald Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Rosenwald_Fellowship "Julius Rosenwald Fellowship"), which came with $1,400 and the purpose of travelling to Scandinavian countries to study agriculture and cooperatives.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

In 1939 [Fort Valley High and Industrial School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley_High_and_Industrial_School "Fort Valley High and Industrial School") was consolidated with the Teacher College and became Fort Valley College. With expansion and addition of programs, in 1996, it became chartered as Fort Valley University.

### Farm Credit Administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Farm Credit Administration")]

Under [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")'s [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal"), many administrations and committees were created. One such administration was the [Farm Credit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farm_Credit_Administration "Farm Credit Administration"), (originally named the [Federal Farm Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Farm_Board "Federal Farm Board")), which had the purpose of providing governmental support to farmers. [Henry Morgenthau Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Morgenthau_Jr. "Henry Morgenthau Jr.") was appointed as governor of the Farm Credit Administration. Morgenthau wanted an African-American man to assist him with his work, and in particular, spread awareness of the administration throughout the African-American farming population.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Du_Bois-1940-5) Hunt moved to Washington D.C. to fulfill the position of Assistant Governor of the Farm Credit Administration in November 1933.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) Hunt maintained his position as principal of Fort Valley High and Industrial School, and Florence remained in Fort Valley to attend to the school.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Fort_Valley_State_University_History-13) As Assistant Governor of the Farm Credit Administration, Hunt travelled often to connect with African-American farmers and inform them of credit unions. A memorandum from Hunt's office in Washington D.C. summarizes some of his research goals while holding the position in the Farm Credit Administration:

> To publicize the work and service of the Farm Credit Administration among Negro farmers in the United States, and to answer letters of inquiry from Negro farmers on all phases of Farm Credit Administration service, explaining to them the procedure involved in applying for credit through the various lending agencies operating under the supervision of the Farm Credit Administration. Also to act as an organizing agent for the Credit Union Section by meeting eligible groups of Negroes, explaining to them the aims and methods of the Federal Credit Act, and assisting in the preliminary steps for establishing credit unions.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

On November 22, 1933, shortly after his appointment to Assistant Governor of the Farm Credit Administration, Hunt wrote a letter to W. E. B. Du Bois, a personal friend of his for more than 25 years of his life.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Du_Bois-1940-5) In this letter Hunt expresses gratitude to Du Bois for Du Bois's recommendation of Hunt to Morgenthau. Even so, soon after his appointment, Hunt had already been writing letters to various institutions and administrations across the nation involved in the improvement of African-American farmers' lives.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-14)

On February 7, 1934, Hunt was called to attend the Interdepartmental Group Concerned with Special Problems of Negroes, colloquially known as [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")'s [Black Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Cabinet "Black Cabinet").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-15) He was one of a total of 45 African Americans who created federal policy on education, jobs and housing at major cabinet-level agencies in the executive branch. They also acted as Roosevelt's informal advisers on national issues related to African Americans and the [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal"). In 1935, a sub-committee of this Interdepartmental Group Concerned with Special Problems of Negroes, specifically dedicated to agriculture was formed of Hunt and four other men.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

Hunt has also been credited as largely responsible for the creation of Flint River Farms, which was established in [Macon County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macon_County,_Georgia "Macon County, Georgia"), Georgia, in 1937.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-16) The Flint River Farms was founded as a cooperative community for African-American farmers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

Hunt died on October 1, 1938.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Fort_Valley_State_University_History-13)

## Legacy and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legacy and honors")]

*   1930 - [Spingarn Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal "Spingarn Medal")
    *   In 1930, Hunt received major awards for his 25 years of service in the education of black students.

*   1930 - Harmon Award - [William E. Harmon Foundation award for distinguished achievement among Negroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_E._Harmon_Foundation_award_for_distinguished_achievement_among_Negroes "William E. Harmon Foundation award for distinguished achievement among Negroes"), for education

Henry Alexander Hunt High School in Fort Valley was named for him. Fort Valley State University's main library is named for him.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-17)
