[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Portrait_of_Henry_Alexander_Hunt.png/250px-Portrait_of_Henry_Alexander_Hunt.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_Henry_Alexander_Hunt.png)

A photo of Henry Alexander Hunt featured in the August 1930 edition of _[The Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crisis "The Crisis")_ magazine. The photo accompanied an article discussing Hunt being awarded the 16th [Spingarn Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal "Spingarn Medal").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-1)

**Henry Alexander Hunt** (October 10, 1866[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-2)– October 1, 1938) was an American educator who led efforts to reach blacks in rural areas of Georgia. He was awarded the [Spingarn Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal "Spingarn Medal") by the [National Association for the Advancement of Colored People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People "National Association for the Advancement of Colored People") (NAACP), as well as the Harmon Prize. In addition, he was recruited in the 1930s by President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") to join the president's [Black Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Cabinet "Black Cabinet"), an informal group of more than 40 prominent African Americans appointed to positions in the executive agencies.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Henry A. Hunt was born on October 10, 1866, to parents Henry Alexander Hunt Sr. and Mariah Hunt.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-3) He was born on "Hunt Hill", by the small town of Sparta, in [Hancock County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hancock_County,_Georgia "Hancock County, Georgia"), part of the [Black Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Belt_(geological_formation) "Black Belt (geological formation)"). Hunt was the youngest of eight children, four boys and four girls, born to an African-American mother, Mariah Hunt. The Hunts lived in a weather-beaten house on their small farm and the children grew up working on the farm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) Despite his African-American roots, Hunt's appearance led people to assume he was from purely Caucasian descent. After Hunt's death, [W. E. B. Du Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois "W. E. B. Du Bois"), a personal friend of his, publicly spoke of Hunt's Caucasian appearance and reflected on the questions Hunt received about why he did not choose to hide his mixed-race background.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Du_Bois-1940-5)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]

He attended school at Sparta for his early education. In 1882, at the age of 16, he started at [Atlanta University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_University "Atlanta University") (now Clark Atlanta University), one of the [historically black colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges "Historically black colleges") created after the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6) While attending [Atlanta University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Atlanta_University "Clark Atlanta University"), Hunt met Florence Johnson, the woman he would eventually marry in 1893.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-van_Hartesveldt-2015-7)[Edward A. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_A._Johnson "Edward A. Johnson"), Florence's brother, was the former Assemblyman of New York.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Horne%E2%80%931930-8)

Throughout his time as a college student, including vacations from school, Hunt worked as a carpenter to earn money.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) Hunt graduated from [Atlanta University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Atlanta_University "Clark Atlanta University") with a Bachelors of Arts degree and completion of coursework in the Industrial Department in 1890.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early career")]

Hunt worked for the education of black students for his entire career. After graduating, he had a job offer in Africa, but he turned this down to be the principal at Charlotte Grade School in Charlotte, North Carolina.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) He stayed at this position for less than a year, leaving the Charlotte Grade School in 1891 for the position of Superintendent of the Industrial Department at [Biddle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biddle_University "Biddle University") (now [Johnson C. Smith University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_C._Smith_University "Johnson C. Smith University")). In the year 1900, Hunt established an annual African-American farmer's conference including the counties surrounding Charlotte, North Carolina.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Culp-1902-6) Hunt continued to work for [Biddle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biddle_University "Biddle University") for the rest of the thirteen and a half years the Hunts were in Charlotte, North Carolina.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) By the time he left Biddle University, he had also been appointed as Superintendent of Boarding.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9)

### Fort Valley career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Fort Valley career")]

He was then the principal of [Fort Valley High and Industrial School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley_High_and_Industrial_School "Fort Valley High and Industrial School"), [Fort Valley, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley,_Georgia "Fort Valley, Georgia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Horne%E2%80%931930-8)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-10) The [Fort Valley High and Industrial School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley_High_and_Industrial_School "Fort Valley High and Industrial School"), affiliated with the American Church Institute of the [Protestant Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)"), was chartered in 1895, but struggled financially.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-11) The school received funds from Northern philanthropists, but there were disagreements about whether the school should pursue a Liberal Arts educational model or the Hampton-Tuskegee Industrial educational model.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) In the 1902–1903 school year, the school's first principal, John W. Davis was released as principal and the trustees began looking for replacements.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) George Foster Peabody, one of Fort Valley's Northern philantrhopists who was on the Board of Trustees, suggested Hunt because of his work at Biddle University. Other trustees had suggested different men for the position of principal, and although Hunt was among the final three candidates, he was only offered the position after the other two had declined the job.

Even after this, Hunt did not immediately get the job. The trustees were reluctant to hire an Atlanta University graduate since [Booker T. Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._Washington "Booker T. Washington") had advised the board of trustees that an Industrial College not run by a [Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_University "Hampton University") or [Tuskegee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_University "Tuskegee University") graduate, was not likely to be successful.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) The 1903 school year began for Fort Valley High and Industrial School began without a principal as the trustees continued to scrutinize Hunt. Hunt stressed the mechanical background he acquired from his industrial studies at Atlanta University and his background in carpentry and was then hired in November 1903.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) The Hunts moved to Fort Valley with their three small children, two girls and one boy, and Hunt began his career as the Fort Valley High and Industrial School principal on February 9, 1904.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9)

When the Hunts came to the school it consisted of a single building, Odd Fellows Lodge, and the school had an annual budget of $840.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-van_Hartesveldt-2015-7) The Hunts lived with no running water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-van_Hartesveldt-2015-7) Hunt began to change the school's educational model to aim more towards vocational training and trade-based studies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) Hunt instated classes in sewing, cooking, carpentry, and gardening. Hunt also planted two hundred peach trees (Fort Valley is located in what is known as the [Peach Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Belt_Conference "Peach Belt Conference")) to expand the agricultural program to include practical and demonstrative agricultural education.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) Hunt felt a focus on agricultural studies was important given the emphasis on and prevalence of agriculture in middle Georgia, where the school was located. In the beginning and throughout Hunt's career the area surrounding the school was dominated by a population of African Americans who worked in agriculture. Hunt often stated his goal as empowering the African Americans attending Fort Valley, as well as the surrounding African-American community, to become effective in their trade.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9)

> With Negroes cultivating millions of acres of land, surely no argument is needed to prove the wisdom and the justice of giving them every possible opportunity to learn how to do that work more intelligently and with greater skill.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

In 1907, Hunt presented to the Board of Trustees the need to add the study of scientific agricultural training to the existing agricultural studies program.

> Working as we do among a people who are engaged very largely in agriculture it would seem to be not only important but absolutely necessary that special inducements be held out to students who wish to give attention to this particular line of work.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

Also in 1907, Hunt began an annual Fort Valley conference for African American farmers. The conference brought experts from throughout the state, the country and some of the top industrial schools such as [Tuskegee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_University "Tuskegee University"), to inform the attendees of the latest agricultural technology and information. At these conferences, Hunt stressed the possibility for African-American farmers to own their farms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) In 1907, Hunt also began a practical agricultural program, with the help of the [United States Department of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture "United States Department of Agriculture"), five acres of land were cultivated and used as part of the educational process through demonstrations.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) With financial help from the General Board of Education, Hunt added 55 acres to the school's educational farmland in 1915.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Anderson-1988-9) Hunt's reputation as an advocate for the African-American farmer spread. In 1918, the Governor of Georgia, [Hugh M. Dorsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Dorsey "Hugh Dorsey"), appointed Hunt to the position of supervisor of Negro economics for the state of Georgia. In this position Hunt focused on problems relating to agricultural labor in Georgia.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

In 1925, [W. E. B. Du Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois "W. E. B. Du Bois") asked for Hunt's help with a research project focused on the study of Negro Common Schools in Georgia. In a response letter to Du Bois, Hunt expressed interest but ultimately declined the offer because he was busy overseeing the building of a boy's dormitory on the Fort Valley campus.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-12)

In 1930, Hunt was awarded the 16th Spingarn Medal for his 25 years of work in Fort Valley. When he started working for Fort Valley High and Industrial School there was only one building. Over the years, he raised funds to build the plant of the school and turned it into a community center of teaching about health and farming, as well as academic subjects, and built relations with the regional community of 300,000 blacks and whites. The result of this was a campus expanded to 12 buildings, 91 acres of land, and a worth of $450,000 in 1930.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Horne%E2%80%931930-8) In 1931 Hunt received the [Julius Rosenwald Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Rosenwald_Fellowship "Julius Rosenwald Fellowship"), which came with $1,400 and the purpose of travelling to Scandinavian countries to study agriculture and cooperatives.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

In 1939 [Fort Valley High and Industrial School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Valley_High_and_Industrial_School "Fort Valley High and Industrial School") was consolidated with the Teacher College and became Fort Valley College. With expansion and addition of programs, in 1996, it became chartered as Fort Valley University.

### Farm Credit Administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_A._Hunt&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Farm Credit Administration")]

Under [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")'s [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal"), many administrations and committees were created. One such administration was the [Farm Credit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farm_Credit_Administration "Farm Credit Administration"), (originally named the [Federal Farm Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Farm_Board "Federal Farm Board")), which had the purpose of providing governmental support to farmers. [Henry Morgenthau Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Morgenthau_Jr. "Henry Morgenthau Jr.") was appointed as governor of the Farm Credit Administration. Morgenthau wanted an African-American man to assist him with his work, and in particular, spread awareness of the administration throughout the African-American farming population.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Du_Bois-1940-5) Hunt moved to Washington D.C. to fulfill the position of Assistant Governor of the Farm Credit Administration in November 1933.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4) Hunt maintained his position as principal of Fort Valley High and Industrial School, and Florence remained in Fort Valley to attend to the school.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Fort_Valley_State_University_History-13) As Assistant Governor of the Farm Credit Administration, Hunt travelled often to connect with African-American farmers and inform them of credit unions. A memorandum from Hunt's office in Washington D.C. summarizes some of his research goals while holding the position in the Farm Credit Administration:

> To publicize the work and service of the Farm Credit Administration among Negro farmers in the United States, and to answer letters of inquiry from Negro farmers on all phases of Farm Credit Administration service, explaining to them the procedure involved in applying for credit through the various lending agencies operating under the supervision of the Farm Credit Administration. Also to act as an organizing agent for the Credit Union Section by meeting eligible groups of Negroes, explaining to them the aims and methods of the Federal Credit Act, and assisting in the preliminary steps for establishing credit unions.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

On November 22, 1933, shortly after his appointment to Assistant Governor of the Farm Credit Administration, Hunt wrote a letter to W. E. B. Du Bois, a personal friend of his for more than 25 years of his life.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Du_Bois-1940-5) In this letter Hunt expresses gratitude to Du Bois for Du Bois's recommendation of Hunt to Morgenthau. Even so, soon after his appointment, Hunt had already been writing letters to various institutions and administrations across the nation involved in the improvement of African-American farmers' lives.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-14)

On February 7, 1934, Hunt was called to attend the Interdepartmental Group Concerned with Special Problems of Negroes, colloquially known as [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")'s [Black Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Cabinet "Black Cabinet").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-15) He was one of a total of 45 African Americans who created federal policy on education, jobs and housing at major cabinet-level agencies in the executive branch. They also acted as Roosevelt's informal advisers on national issues related to African Americans and the [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal"). In 1935, a sub-committee of this Interdepartmental Group Concerned with Special Problems of Negroes, specifically dedicated to agriculture was formed of Hunt and four other men.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

Hunt has also been credited as largely responsible for the creation of Flint River Farms, which was established in [Macon County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macon_County,_Georgia "Macon County, Georgia"), Georgia, in 1937.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-16) The Flint River Farms was founded as a cooperative community for African-American farmers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Bellamy-1975-4)

Hunt died on October 1, 1938.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-Fort_Valley_State_University_History-13)

## Legacy and honors

*   1930 - [Spingarn Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal "Spingarn Medal")
    *   In 1930, Hunt received major awards for his 25 years of service in the education of black students.

*   1930 - Harmon Award - [William E. Harmon Foundation award for distinguished achievement among Negroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_E._Harmon_Foundation_award_for_distinguished_achievement_among_Negroes "William E. Henry Alexander Hunt High School in Fort Valley was named for him. Fort Valley State University's main library is named for him.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Hunt#cite_note-17)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

NAACP award for the highest achievement of an American of African descent

The **Spingarn Medal** is awarded annually by the [National Association for the Advancement of Colored People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP "NAACP") (NAACP) for an outstanding achievement by an [Black American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans"). The award was created in 1914 by [Joel Elias Spingarn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Elias_Spingarn "Joel Elias Spingarn"), chairman of the board of directors of the NAACP.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal#cite_note-Britannica-1) It was first awarded to biologist [Ernest E. Just](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Everett_Just "Ernest Everett Just") in 1915, and has been given most years thereafter.

At its annual convention, the NAACP presents the award after deciding from open nominations. Should the organization end, it would be managed by [Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_University "Howard University") or [Fisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University") Universities.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal#cite_note-Britannica-1) The gold medal is valued at $100, and Spingarn left $20,000 (equivalent to $463,000 in 2025) in his will for the NAACP to continue giving it indefinitely.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal#cite_note-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

NAACP award for the highest achievement of an American of African descent

The **Spingarn Medal** is awarded annually by the [National Association for the Advancement of Colored People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP "NAACP") (NAACP) for an outstanding achievement by an [Black American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans"). The award was created in 1914 by [Joel Elias Spingarn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Elias_Spingarn "Joel Elias Spingarn"), chairman of the board of directors of the NAACP.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal#cite_note-Britannica-1) It was first awarded to biologist [Ernest E. Just](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Everett_Just "Ernest Everett Just") in 1915, and has been given most years thereafter.

At its annual convention, the NAACP presents the award after deciding from open nominations. Should the organization end, it would be managed by [Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_University "Howard University") or [Fisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University") Universities.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal#cite_note-Britannica-1) The gold medal is valued at $100, and Spingarn left $20,000 (equivalent to $463,000 in 2025) in his will for the NAACP to continue giving it indefinitely.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spingarn_Medal#cite_note-2)

**Morrow** is a [village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_(United_States)#Ohio "Village (United States)") in [Salem Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem_Township,_Warren_County,_Ohio "Salem Township, Warren County, Ohio"), [Warren County, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_County,_Ohio "Warren County, Ohio"), United States. The population was 2,049 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Morrow was [platted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plat "Plat") in 1845, when the railroad was extended to that point.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-4) The village is named for [Jeremiah Morrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_Morrow "Jeremiah Morrow"), 9th [Governor of Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Ohio "List of governors of Ohio").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-5) A post office has been in operation at Morrow since 1845.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-6)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), the village has a total area of 1.97 square miles (5.10 km 2), of which 1.93 square miles (5.00 km 2) is land and 0.04 square miles (0.10 km 2) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-Gazetteer_files-7)

### 2010 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2010 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-wwwcensusgov-9) of 2010, there were 1,188 people, 455 households, and 298 families living in the village. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") was 615.5 inhabitants per square mile (237.6/km 2). There were 522 housing units at an average density of 270.5 per square mile (104.4/km 2). The racial makeup of the village was 96.5% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_(U.S._Census) "White (U.S. Census)"), 0.4% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_(U.S._Census) "African American (U.S. Census)"), 0.2% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_(U.S._Census) "Native American (U.S. Census)"), 0.3% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_(U.S._Census) "Asian (U.S. Census)"), 0.6% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(U.S._Census) "Race (U.S. Census)"), and 2.0% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_(U.S._Census) "Hispanic (U.S. Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_(U.S._Census) "Latino (U.S. Census)") of any race were 2.0% of the population.

There were 455 households, of which 36.3% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 45.5% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 13.4% had a female householder with no husband present, 6.6% had a male householder with no wife present, and 34.5% were non-families. Of all households 29.0% were made up of individuals, and 17.6% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.53 and the average family size was 3.07.

The median age in the village was 39 years. 24.8% of residents were under the age of 18; 6.7% were between the ages of 18 and 24; 26.7% were from 25 to 44; 26% were from 45 to 64; and 15.8% were 65 years of age or older. The gender makeup of the village was 48.2% male and 51.8% female.

### 2000 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2000 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-GR2-3) of 2000, there were 1,286 people, 462 households, and 298 families living in the village. The population density was 760.7 inhabitants per square mile (293.7/km 2). There were 498 housing units at an average density of 294.6 per square mile (113.7/km 2). The racial makeup of the village was 97.82% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_(U.S._Census) "White (U.S. Census)"), 0.70% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_(U.S._Census) "African American (U.S. Census)"), 0.86% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_(U.S._Census) "Native American (U.S. Census)"), 0.08% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_(U.S._Census) "Asian (U.S. Census)"), 0.16% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), and 0.39% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_(U.S._Census) "Hispanic (U.S. Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_(U.S._Census) "Latino (U.S. Census)") of any race were 2.18% of the population.

There were 462 households, out of which 34.0% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 47.4% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 14.1% had a female householder with no husband present, and 35.3% were non-families. Of all households 29.0% were made up of individuals, and 14.5% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.58 and the average family size was 3.19.

In the village, the population was spread out, with 25.6% under the age of 18, 6.6% from 18 to 24, 30.6% from 25 to 44, 21.4% from 45 to 64, and 15.9% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 37 years. For every 100 females there were 85.8 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 83.0 males.

The median income for a household in the village was $32,566, and the median income for a family was $44,750. Males had a median income of $31,827 versus $24,444 for females. The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income "Per capita income") for the village was $15,416. About 5.2% of families and 15.5% of the population were below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line "Poverty line"), including 10.1% of those under age 18 and 11.1% of those age 65 or over.

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Education")]

The village is in the [Little Miami Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Miami_Schools "Little Miami Schools").

The Salem Township Public Library is a lending library located within the village limits.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-10)

## Government and infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Government and infrastructure")]

The Morrow Post Office of the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") is located at 531 West Pike Street.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-11)

The village has a 1% income tax.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-Morrow_Tax_Department-12)

## Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Music")]

*   The town is the subject of a song called "[I Want to Go to Morrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Want_to_Go_to_Morrow "I Want to Go to Morrow")", about a man who wishes to take a train "to Morrow" and return "tomorrow" night, playing on the similar pronunciations of the two phrases. An early recording of the song, by [Dan W. Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_W._Quinn "Dan W. Quinn"), was released in 1903.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-13) The song was popularly recorded by [The Kingston Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kingston_Trio "The Kingston Trio").

**Morrow** is a [village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_(United_States)#Ohio "Village (United States)") in [Salem Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem_Township,_Warren_County,_Ohio "Salem Township, Warren County, Ohio"), [Warren County, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_County,_Ohio "Warren County, Ohio"), United States. The population was 2,049 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Morrow was [platted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plat "Plat") in 1845, when the railroad was extended to that point.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-4) The village is named for [Jeremiah Morrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_Morrow "Jeremiah Morrow"), 9th [Governor of Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Ohio "List of governors of Ohio").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-5) A post office has been in operation at Morrow since 1845.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-6)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), the village has a total area of 1.97 square miles (5.10 km 2), of which 1.93 square miles (5.00 km 2) is land and 0.04 square miles (0.10 km 2) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-Gazetteer_files-7)

### 2010 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2010 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-wwwcensusgov-9) of 2010, there were 1,188 people, 455 households, and 298 families living in the village. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") was 615.5 inhabitants per square mile (237.6/km 2). There were 522 housing units at an average density of 270.5 per square mile (104.4/km 2). The racial makeup of the village was 96.5% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_(U.S._Census) "White (U.S. Census)"), 0.4% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_(U.S._Census) "African American (U.S. Census)"), 0.2% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_(U.S._Census) "Native American (U.S. Census)"), 0.3% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_(U.S._Census) "Asian (U.S. Census)"), 0.6% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(U.S._Census) "Race (U.S. Census)"), and 2.0% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_(U.S._Census) "Hispanic (U.S. Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_(U.S._Census) "Latino (U.S. Census)") of any race were 2.0% of the population.

There were 455 households, of which 36.3% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 45.5% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 13.4% had a female householder with no husband present, 6.6% had a male householder with no wife present, and 34.5% were non-families. Of all households 29.0% were made up of individuals, and 17.6% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.53 and the average family size was 3.07.

The median age in the village was 39 years. 24.8% of residents were under the age of 18; 6.7% were between the ages of 18 and 24; 26.7% were from 25 to 44; 26% were from 45 to 64; and 15.8% were 65 years of age or older. The gender makeup of the village was 48.2% male and 51.8% female.

### 2000 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2000 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-GR2-3) of 2000, there were 1,286 people, 462 households, and 298 families living in the village. The population density was 760.7 inhabitants per square mile (293.7/km 2). There were 498 housing units at an average density of 294.6 per square mile (113.7/km 2). The racial makeup of the village was 97.82% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_(U.S._Census) "White (U.S. Census)"), 0.70% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_(U.S._Census) "African American (U.S. Census)"), 0.86% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_(U.S._Census) "Native American (U.S. Census)"), 0.08% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_(U.S._Census) "Asian (U.S. Census)"), 0.16% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), and 0.39% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_(U.S._Census) "Hispanic (U.S. Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_(U.S._Census) "Latino (U.S. Census)") of any race were 2.18% of the population.

There were 462 households, out of which 34.0% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 47.4% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 14.1% had a female householder with no husband present, and 35.3% were non-families. Of all households 29.0% were made up of individuals, and 14.5% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.58 and the average family size was 3.19.

In the village, the population was spread out, with 25.6% under the age of 18, 6.6% from 18 to 24, 30.6% from 25 to 44, 21.4% from 45 to 64, and 15.9% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 37 years. For every 100 females there were 85.8 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 83.0 males.

The median income for a household in the village was $32,566, and the median income for a family was $44,750. Males had a median income of $31,827 versus $24,444 for females. The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income "Per capita income") for the village was $15,416. About 5.2% of families and 15.5% of the population were below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line "Poverty line"), including 10.1% of those under age 18 and 11.1% of those age 65 or over.

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Education")]

The village is in the [Little Miami Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Miami_Schools "Little Miami Schools").

The Salem Township Public Library is a lending library located within the village limits.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-10)

## Government and infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Government and infrastructure")]

The Morrow Post Office of the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") is located at 531 West Pike Street.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-11)

The village has a 1% income tax.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-Morrow_Tax_Department-12)

## Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morrow,_Ohio&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Music")]

*   The town is the subject of a song called "[I Want to Go to Morrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Want_to_Go_to_Morrow "I Want to Go to Morrow")", about a man who wishes to take a train "to Morrow" and return "tomorrow" night, playing on the similar pronunciations of the two phrases. An early recording of the song, by [Dan W. Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_W._Quinn "Dan W. Quinn"), was released in 1903.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrow,_Ohio#cite_note-13) The song was popularly recorded by [The Kingston Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kingston_Trio "The Kingston Trio").

The **NAACP Image Awards** is an annual awards ceremony presented by the American-based National Association for the Advancement of Colored People ([NAACP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP "NAACP")) to honor outstanding performances in film, television, theatre, music, and literature. Over 40 categories of the Image Awards are voted on by the NAACP members. Honorary awards (similar to the [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award")) have also been included, such as the [President's Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_%E2%80%93_President's_Award "NAACP Image Award – President's Award"), the [Chairman's Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_%E2%80%93_Chairman's_Award "NAACP Image Award – Chairman's Award"), the [Entertainer of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_for_Entertainer_of_the_Year "NAACP Image Award for Entertainer of the Year"), the [Activist of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_for_Activist_of_the_Year "NAACP Image Award for Activist of the Year"), and the [Hall of Fame Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_%E2%80%93_Hall_of_Fame_Award "NAACP Image Award – Hall of Fame Award"). [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyonc%C3%A9 "Beyoncé") is the most awarded individual with 25 wins as a solo artist.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NAACP_Image_Awards&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The [awards ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awards_ceremony "Awards ceremony") was conceived by [Toni Vaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toni_Vaz "Toni Vaz")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-1) during an April 1967 NAACP branch meeting in Beverly Hills. Vaz named it the Image Awards as she "wanted a better image for the people who worked in the industry," and wanted to "put this award show together to thank the producers for giving good roles to people of color." Vaz stated that the branch president liked the idea, but when she called members and friends to enlist volunteers for an awards show committee, no one volunteered. Vaz then contacted numerous Black celebrities such as [Sammy Davis Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Davis_Jr. "Sammy Davis Jr."), who hosted the first meeting of the NAACP Beverly Hills Hollywood Branch in his home; [Sidney Poitier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Poitier "Sidney Poitier"), whom she had worked with on the film _[Porgy and Bess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porgy\_and\_Bess\_(film) "Porgy and Bess (film)")_; and [Ivan Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Dixon "Ivan Dixon"), an actor, director and producer of _[Hogan's Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogan's\_Heroes "Hogan's Heroes")_ at the time. Vaz also wrote letters to secure sponsors for the event and booked the Beverly Hilton Hotel, where the first NAACP Image Awards show was held on August 13, 1967. The ceremony was presented by activists [Maggie Hathaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maggie_Hathaway "Maggie Hathaway"), Sammy Davis Jr. and Willis Edwards, all three of whom were leaders of the Beverly Hills-Hollywood NAACP branch.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-first-3)

Due to changes in timing of the awards, no awards ceremony was held the following years:

*   1973, as the timing was changed to honor a full calendar year early in the following year.
*   1979, as the 11th annual awards were held in June 1978[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-ap-19780611-4) and the 12th annual awards were held in January 1980.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-awds12th-5) The awards reverted to a "late-in-year" ceremony for 1980 with the 13th annual awards held in December 1980.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-awds13th-6)
*   1991, as the timing returned to early in the following calendar year to honor the previous year's work.
*   1995, when the awards were canceled due to financial concerns.

In 1982, the NAACP Image Awards was televised for the first time with the 15th ceremony.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-loc-15th-7) Initially, the NAACP Image Awards aired locally in Los Angeles on KHJ-TV (currently known as [KCAL-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KCAL-TV "KCAL-TV"))[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2) although the 1982 and 1983 ceremonies were [syndicated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_syndication "Broadcast syndication") nationally.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-8) Willis Edwards, former president of the Beverly Hills/Hollywood Branch of the NAACP, contacted then-[NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") president [Brandon Tartikoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Tartikoff "Brandon Tartikoff") to nationally broadcast the 19th NAACP Image Awards, which was held at [The Wiltern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pellissier_Building_and_Wiltern_Theatre "Pellissier Building and Wiltern Theatre") in Los Angeles on December 14, 1986.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2) The ceremony was broadcast on NBC on January 17, 1987, as a 90-minute special at 11:30 pm, preempting the slot usually filled by _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-9)

Initially, the Image Awards aired in a late night slot on NBC in the weeks when _Saturday Night Live_ did not air a new episode, but in subsequent years, it aired on [primetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime "Primetime") on [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Broadcasting_Company "Fox Broadcasting Company") and continued to air on primetime when it returned to NBC.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-var-20120117-11) The award show aired as a primetime telecast for the first time on April 23, 1996, for its 27th edition as it began its 16-year run on Fox.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-var-20120117-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-primetv1996-12) The award show was broadcast live for the first time on March 2, 2007, for its [38th edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/38th_NAACP_Image_Awards "38th NAACP Image Awards") (the ceremony was broadcast with [tape delay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_delay "Broadcast delay") prior to 2007). The Image Awards returned to NBC for its [43rd edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/43rd_NAACP_Image_Awards "43rd NAACP Image Awards") in 2012.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-var-20120117-11)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-13)

From 2014 to 2018, the Black-owned cable network [TV One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_One_(American_TV_channel) "TV One (American TV channel)") aired the Image Awards. The awards currently air on [BET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BET "BET") with a simulcast on its sister networks including [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2)

The New York firm [Society Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_Awards "Society Awards") manufactures the trophy since its redesign in 2008.

### Cultural impact

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NAACP_Image_Awards&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cultural impact")]

The NAACP Image Awards has received national attention and dubbed as the "_Black_ _[Oscars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy\_Awards "Academy Awards")/[Emmys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime\_Emmy\_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards")/[Grammys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy\_Awards "Grammy Awards")"_ award show from the African-American and Latino community, as it is an important [prestigious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reputation "Reputation") award celebrating artists and entertainers of color that may have been overlooked from by the mainstream film, television, theater and music award counterparts ([EGOT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EGOT "EGOT")) due to racial seclusion or low interest from film and television studios. Whereas, it created more exposure for content on a wide spectrum of urban media versus other awards shows where they can be celebrated and appreciated. Actors such as [Will Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Smith "Will Smith"), [Jada Pinkett-Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jada_Pinkett_Smith "Jada Pinkett Smith"), [Taraji P. Henson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taraji_P._Henson "Taraji P. Henson") and many others expressed the differences of not being visually seen by the industry's standard and how artists and entertainers should look to the NAACP Image Awards as the highest achievement. The campaign of [#OscarSoWhite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OscarsSoWhite "OscarsSoWhite") began as a protest after seeing few people of color being nominated or win in major categories at the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards"). Since then, minor adjustments have been made for inclusion as more people of color have become nominated and win at the mainstream prestigious award ceremonies.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-14)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NAACP_Image_Awards&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Controversies")]

In 1987, the NAACP received criticism for not presenting their Best Actress award for that year. They defended this position, citing a lack of meaningful roles for Black women.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-36) In 1990, they were criticized once again for not awarding Best Actress.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-NAACP_Best_Actress-37) This was the fourth time it could not find enough nominees for Best Actress.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-NAACP_Best_Actress-37) Sandra Evers-Manly, president of the organization's Beverly Hills/Hollywood branch, said, "The [film] industry has yet to show diversity or present realistic leading roles for [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") women."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-NAACP_Best_Actress-37)

In several instances, nominees have been perceived as "undeserving" or "unworthy" of recognition by members of the media, fellow celebrities, as well as the general public; in their own defense, some NAACP representatives have stated that the overall quality of an artist's work is the salient issue. This would render certain factors, such as criminal charges or the nominee's history, being inconsequential in this regard. For example, in 1994, rapper [Tupac Shakur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupac_Shakur "Tupac Shakur") was nominated for Outstanding Actor in a Motion Picture (for _[Poetic Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetic\_Justice\_(film) "Poetic Justice (film)")_), despite [sexual assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_assault "Sexual assault") charges being filed against him in December 1993.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-38) Furthermore, Shakur had been accused of felony counts of forcible sodomy and unlawful detainment in New York City; a woman alleged that he and two male accomplices held her captive, in a hotel room, and restricted her movements, holding her down as a fourth accomplice sodomized her.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-Charged-39) Shakur was also indicted for two counts of aggravated assault, in an unrelated incident, in which he supposedly shot and wounded two off-duty police officers.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-Charged-39) The same year, [Martin Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lawrence "Martin Lawrence") was criticized for winning Outstanding Actor in a Comedy Series and Outstanding Comedy Series for _[Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin\_(TV\_series) "Martin (TV series)")_, after Lawrence had been banned from _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_ due to sexual content in his opening monologue.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-Charged-39) In 2004, [R. Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Kelly "R. Kelly")'s _[Chocolate Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolate\_Factory "Chocolate Factory")_ was nominated for Outstanding Album[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-40) while he was under [indictment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indictment "Indictment") for charges related to [child pornography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_pornography "Child pornography").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-zahn-41)

Other nominees have faced controversy due to their portrayals of major civil rights figures. In 2003, the comedy film _[Barbershop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbershop\_(film) "Barbershop (film)")_ received five nominations, including Outstanding Motion Picture and Outstanding Supporting Actor (for [Cedric the Entertainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedric_the_Entertainer "Cedric the Entertainer")'s performance); during the film, Cedric's character makes [pejorative remarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbershop_(film)#Subjects_discussed_in_the_barbershop "Barbershop (film)") about [Rosa Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Parks "Rosa Parks"), [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson"), and [Jesse Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Jackson "Jesse Jackson"). This content caused criticism, including Parks' refusal to attend the ceremony.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-42) Hip-hop group [Outkast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outkast "Outkast") received six nominations in 2004, and criticism soon followed, for both them and the NAACP, due to the name of one of their songs being "[Rosa Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Parks_(song) "Rosa Parks (song)")". The song had resulted in [Parks suing OutKast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parks_v._LaFace_Records "Parks v. LaFace Records") for defamation over use of her name.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-zahn-41)

The **NAACP Image Awards** is an annual awards ceremony presented by the American-based National Association for the Advancement of Colored People ([NAACP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP "NAACP")) to honor outstanding performances in film, television, theatre, music, and literature. Over 40 categories of the Image Awards are voted on by the NAACP members. Honorary awards (similar to the [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award")) have also been included, such as the [President's Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_%E2%80%93_President's_Award "NAACP Image Award – President's Award"), the [Chairman's Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_%E2%80%93_Chairman's_Award "NAACP Image Award – Chairman's Award"), the [Entertainer of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_for_Entertainer_of_the_Year "NAACP Image Award for Entertainer of the Year"), the [Activist of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_for_Activist_of_the_Year "NAACP Image Award for Activist of the Year"), and the [Hall of Fame Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Image_Award_%E2%80%93_Hall_of_Fame_Award "NAACP Image Award – Hall of Fame Award"). [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyonc%C3%A9 "Beyoncé") is the most awarded individual with 25 wins as a solo artist.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NAACP_Image_Awards&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The [awards ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awards_ceremony "Awards ceremony") was conceived by [Toni Vaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toni_Vaz "Toni Vaz")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-1) during an April 1967 NAACP branch meeting in Beverly Hills. Vaz named it the Image Awards as she "wanted a better image for the people who worked in the industry," and wanted to "put this award show together to thank the producers for giving good roles to people of color." Vaz stated that the branch president liked the idea, but when she called members and friends to enlist volunteers for an awards show committee, no one volunteered. Vaz then contacted numerous Black celebrities such as [Sammy Davis Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Davis_Jr. "Sammy Davis Jr."), who hosted the first meeting of the NAACP Beverly Hills Hollywood Branch in his home; [Sidney Poitier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Poitier "Sidney Poitier"), whom she had worked with on the film _[Porgy and Bess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porgy\_and\_Bess\_(film) "Porgy and Bess (film)")_; and [Ivan Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Dixon "Ivan Dixon"), an actor, director and producer of _[Hogan's Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogan's\_Heroes "Hogan's Heroes")_ at the time. Vaz also wrote letters to secure sponsors for the event and booked the Beverly Hilton Hotel, where the first NAACP Image Awards show was held on August 13, 1967. The ceremony was presented by activists [Maggie Hathaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maggie_Hathaway "Maggie Hathaway"), Sammy Davis Jr. and Willis Edwards, all three of whom were leaders of the Beverly Hills-Hollywood NAACP branch.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-first-3)

Due to changes in timing of the awards, no awards ceremony was held the following years:

*   1973, as the timing was changed to honor a full calendar year early in the following year.
*   1979, as the 11th annual awards were held in June 1978[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-ap-19780611-4) and the 12th annual awards were held in January 1980.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-awds12th-5) The awards reverted to a "late-in-year" ceremony for 1980 with the 13th annual awards held in December 1980.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-awds13th-6)
*   1991, as the timing returned to early in the following calendar year to honor the previous year's work.
*   1995, when the awards were canceled due to financial concerns.

In 1982, the NAACP Image Awards was televised for the first time with the 15th ceremony.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-loc-15th-7) Initially, the NAACP Image Awards aired locally in Los Angeles on KHJ-TV (currently known as [KCAL-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KCAL-TV "KCAL-TV"))[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2) although the 1982 and 1983 ceremonies were [syndicated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_syndication "Broadcast syndication") nationally.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-8) Willis Edwards, former president of the Beverly Hills/Hollywood Branch of the NAACP, contacted then-[NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") president [Brandon Tartikoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Tartikoff "Brandon Tartikoff") to nationally broadcast the 19th NAACP Image Awards, which was held at [The Wiltern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pellissier_Building_and_Wiltern_Theatre "Pellissier Building and Wiltern Theatre") in Los Angeles on December 14, 1986.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2) The ceremony was broadcast on NBC on January 17, 1987, as a 90-minute special at 11:30 pm, preempting the slot usually filled by _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-9)

Initially, the Image Awards aired in a late night slot on NBC in the weeks when _Saturday Night Live_ did not air a new episode, but in subsequent years, it aired on [primetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime "Primetime") on [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Broadcasting_Company "Fox Broadcasting Company") and continued to air on primetime when it returned to NBC.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-var-20120117-11) The award show aired as a primetime telecast for the first time on April 23, 1996, for its 27th edition as it began its 16-year run on Fox.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-var-20120117-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-primetv1996-12) The award show was broadcast live for the first time on March 2, 2007, for its [38th edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/38th_NAACP_Image_Awards "38th NAACP Image Awards") (the ceremony was broadcast with [tape delay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_delay "Broadcast delay") prior to 2007). The Image Awards returned to NBC for its [43rd edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/43rd_NAACP_Image_Awards "43rd NAACP Image Awards") in 2012.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-var-20120117-11)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-13)

From 2014 to 2018, the Black-owned cable network [TV One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_One_(American_TV_channel) "TV One (American TV channel)") aired the Image Awards. The awards currently air on [BET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BET "BET") with a simulcast on its sister networks including [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-naacp-history-2)

The New York firm [Society Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_Awards "Society Awards") manufactures the trophy since its redesign in 2008.

### Cultural impact

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NAACP_Image_Awards&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cultural impact")]

The NAACP Image Awards has received national attention and dubbed as the "_Black_ _[Oscars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy\_Awards "Academy Awards")/[Emmys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime\_Emmy\_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards")/[Grammys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy\_Awards "Grammy Awards")"_ award show from the African-American and Latino community, as it is an important [prestigious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reputation "Reputation") award celebrating artists and entertainers of color that may have been overlooked from by the mainstream film, television, theater and music award counterparts ([EGOT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EGOT "EGOT")) due to racial seclusion or low interest from film and television studios. Whereas, it created more exposure for content on a wide spectrum of urban media versus other awards shows where they can be celebrated and appreciated. Actors such as [Will Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Smith "Will Smith"), [Jada Pinkett-Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jada_Pinkett_Smith "Jada Pinkett Smith"), [Taraji P. Henson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taraji_P._Henson "Taraji P. Henson") and many others expressed the differences of not being visually seen by the industry's standard and how artists and entertainers should look to the NAACP Image Awards as the highest achievement. The campaign of [#OscarSoWhite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OscarsSoWhite "OscarsSoWhite") began as a protest after seeing few people of color being nominated or win in major categories at the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards"). Since then, minor adjustments have been made for inclusion as more people of color have become nominated and win at the mainstream prestigious award ceremonies.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-14)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NAACP_Image_Awards&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Controversies")]

In 1987, the NAACP received criticism for not presenting their Best Actress award for that year. They defended this position, citing a lack of meaningful roles for Black women.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-36) In 1990, they were criticized once again for not awarding Best Actress.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-NAACP_Best_Actress-37) This was the fourth time it could not find enough nominees for Best Actress.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-NAACP_Best_Actress-37) Sandra Evers-Manly, president of the organization's Beverly Hills/Hollywood branch, said, "The [film] industry has yet to show diversity or present realistic leading roles for [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") women."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-NAACP_Best_Actress-37)

In several instances, nominees have been perceived as "undeserving" or "unworthy" of recognition by members of the media, fellow celebrities, as well as the general public; in their own defense, some NAACP representatives have stated that the overall quality of an artist's work is the salient issue. This would render certain factors, such as criminal charges or the nominee's history, being inconsequential in this regard. For example, in 1994, rapper [Tupac Shakur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupac_Shakur "Tupac Shakur") was nominated for Outstanding Actor in a Motion Picture (for _[Poetic Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetic\_Justice\_(film) "Poetic Justice (film)")_), despite [sexual assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_assault "Sexual assault") charges being filed against him in December 1993.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-38) Furthermore, Shakur had been accused of felony counts of forcible sodomy and unlawful detainment in New York City; a woman alleged that he and two male accomplices held her captive, in a hotel room, and restricted her movements, holding her down as a fourth accomplice sodomized her.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-Charged-39) Shakur was also indicted for two counts of aggravated assault, in an unrelated incident, in which he supposedly shot and wounded two off-duty police officers.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-Charged-39) The same year, [Martin Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lawrence "Martin Lawrence") was criticized for winning Outstanding Actor in a Comedy Series and Outstanding Comedy Series for _[Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin\_(TV\_series) "Martin (TV series)")_, after Lawrence had been banned from _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_ due to sexual content in his opening monologue.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-Charged-39) In 2004, [R. Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Kelly "R. Kelly")'s _[Chocolate Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolate\_Factory "Chocolate Factory")_ was nominated for Outstanding Album[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-40) while he was under [indictment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indictment "Indictment") for charges related to [child pornography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_pornography "Child pornography").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-zahn-41)

Other nominees have faced controversy due to their portrayals of major civil rights figures. In 2003, the comedy film _[Barbershop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbershop\_(film) "Barbershop (film)")_ received five nominations, including Outstanding Motion Picture and Outstanding Supporting Actor (for [Cedric the Entertainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedric_the_Entertainer "Cedric the Entertainer")'s performance); during the film, Cedric's character makes [pejorative remarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbershop_(film)#Subjects_discussed_in_the_barbershop "Barbershop (film)") about [Rosa Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Parks "Rosa Parks"), [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson"), and [Jesse Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Jackson "Jesse Jackson"). This content caused criticism, including Parks' refusal to attend the ceremony.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-42) Hip-hop group [Outkast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outkast "Outkast") received six nominations in 2004, and criticism soon followed, for both them and the NAACP, due to the name of one of their songs being "[Rosa Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Parks_(song) "Rosa Parks (song)")". The song had resulted in [Parks suing OutKast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parks_v._LaFace_Records "Parks v. LaFace Records") for defamation over use of her name.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Awards#cite_note-zahn-41)
